title: Christmas abroad with the whole family: how to plan it
author: Matt
intro: Taking the whole family away for Christmas means one booking for a dozen people, three generations and a lot of opinions. It can be the best Christmas you've had, or a very expensive argument. Here's how to pick a place, split the cost and keep the day itself feeling like Christmas.
seo_title: Christmas abroad with the whole family: how to plan it
seo_description: Pick a place everyone can reach, agree the budget early, book one big house or apartments close together, and plan Christmas Day itself. Here's how.

sections.heading: The short answer
sections.text:
- **Book by:** the end of summer if you can
- **Best for mixed ages:** the Canaries
- **Stay:** one villa or two nearby
- **Agree first:** budget and who pays what

Christmas is the most expensive week of the year to travel, so the earlier you agree the plan, the more choice you'll have. If you're reading this in November, it's still doable, just with less choice.

sections.heading: Pick a place that works for everyone
sections.text:
With a big family, the right place is the one that suits the oldest and youngest at once. That usually means a short flight, an easy transfer and somewhere you can walk to a café or the sea.

- **Winter sun:** [Tenerife](/destinations/tenerife), [Gran Canaria](/destinations/gran-canaria) and [Lanzarote](/destinations/lanzarote) are about four hours from the UK, on UK time and warm at Christmas.
- **Snow and Santa:** [Rovaniemi](/destinations/rovaniemi) and [Levi](/destinations/levi) are magical for children, but cold, dark and expensive for everyone else.
- **Christmas markets:** [Vienna](/destinations/vienna) or [Cologne](/destinations/cologne) are better for a few nights before Christmas than for the day itself.

If you can't agree, add a shortlist to somewhere.party and let the draw choose. It takes the decision off one person.

sections.heading: Agree the money before anyone books
sections.text:
Most family holiday rows are really about money. Sort it out first, in writing, even if it feels awkward.

- **Set a budget per household,** not one big total, so nobody feels they're paying for someone else's upgrade.
- **Split the house by room or by person.** By room is simpler; by person is fairer when one family has three children and another has none.
- **Decide who pays for Christmas dinner,** the food shop and any days out.
- **Collect deposits early,** so the person who books isn't carrying everyone's money for months.

Our guide to [splitting holiday costs between two families](/blog/how-to-split-holiday-costs-between-two-families) has worked examples.

sections.heading: Where to stay
sections.text:
A big villa or house keeps everyone together for Christmas Day, with a kitchen and a table big enough for all of you. Two or three apartments in the same complex give each household its own space to retreat to, which matters more than you'd think by Boxing Day.

Tip: check the kitchen properly before you book. Ask whether the oven is big enough for a turkey and whether there are enough plates and chairs for everyone, because holiday lets are often set up for six.

sections.heading: Christmas Day itself
sections.text:
Christmas abroad works best when you decide in advance what has to feel like home and what can be different.

- **The meal:** either book a restaurant early, as many run set Christmas menus and fill up, or plan a self-catered dinner and shop on the 23rd.
- **Local traditions:** in Spain and the Canaries, Christmas Eve is the big night, so the 24th can be lively and the 25th quiet.
- **Presents:** pack them unwrapped. Airport security may need to open wrapped gifts in hand luggage, so bring paper and tape and wrap them when you arrive.
- **Quiet time:** plan a few hours apart, especially with teenagers or older relatives who tire easily.

Watch out: some shops and supermarkets close or open short hours on 25 December and 1 January, so stock up the day before.

sections.heading: Flights and timing
sections.text:
Fly together if you can, so nobody is stuck on a later flight. If the family is spread across the country, pick one destination with direct flights from several airports and arrange to meet there.

School holidays push prices up, so check when each family's schools break up and return. Flying on Christmas Eve or Christmas Day itself is often cheaper and quieter, though there are fewer flights. Our guide to a [holiday with grandparents](/blog/how-to-plan-a-holiday-with-grandparents) covers assistance at the airport and pacing the days.

sections.heading: Still deciding?
sections.text: Browse the [Christmas holidays](/destinations/christmas-holidays) and [where to go in December](/destinations/where-to-go-in-december) pages for ideas. When it comes down to two or three places, put them all in somewhere.party, share the link with the family and let the draw decide.

faqs.question: Where is good for a family Christmas abroad?
faqs.answer: The Canaries suit mixed ages best: about four hours from the UK, on UK time and warm at Christmas. Lapland is magical for children but cold and expensive.

faqs.question: How do you split the cost of a family Christmas holiday?
faqs.answer: Agree a budget per household first, then split the accommodation by room or by person, and decide who pays for food and days out before anyone books.

faqs.question: Can you take wrapped Christmas presents on a plane?
faqs.answer: It's best not to. Security may need to unwrap gifts in hand luggage, so pack them unwrapped and wrap them when you arrive.

faqs.question: Is it cheaper to fly on Christmas Day?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. Flights on 24 and 25 December are usually quieter and can be cheaper, though there are fewer of them.
